title: Abbreviations and acronyms
subtitle: e.g., i.e., NB, ASAP, sitcom, et al.
summary: Read and use the abbreviations English writing is full of - Latin ones such as e.g., i.e. and NB, acronyms such as NATO and PIN, blended words such as sitcom and wi-fi, and the academic set from fig. to et al.

lesson.heading: Abbreviations pronounced as individual letters
rows: for example, from the Latin exempli gratia
that is, from the Latin id est
the year of our Lord, from the Latin Anno Domini; many people prefer CE (Common Era)
before Christ; many people prefer BCE (before the Common Era)
note well, from the Latin nota bene; a warning, or a way of pointing out something important
please reply, from the French; used on invitations

lesson.heading: More letter-by-letter abbreviations
rows: identity document - proof of who you are, such as a passport or driving licence
intelligence quotient: a way of measuring intelligence using a system of numbers
Universal Serial Bus: a type of connection between a computer and an electronic device
unidentified flying object; often used to talk about an alien spaceship

lesson.heading: Shortened and blended words
rows: a flat with only one room, which is both a bedroom and a sitting room
situational comedy: a kind of humorous TV programme
biographical data: details about someone's life, job and achievements
biographical picture: a film about the life of a real person
wireless fidelity: wireless connection for computers and electronic communications

lesson.heading: Acronyms
lesson.text: Some abbreviations are **acronyms**: they are formed from the first letters (or occasionally syllables) of a word or series of words, and they are pronounced as a word rather than letter by letter.

examples.text: **PIN** - personal identification number, used on credit and bank cards
**VAT** - value-added tax, a kind of tax on goods
examples.note: said either as one word or letter by letter

lesson.heading: Abbreviations used in academic writing and bibliographies
rows: figure: a picture or drawing, often numbered, in a book or document
editor/editors - the people who oversaw the contents, not the authors
see p. 26; see pp. 58-61 (everything from page 58 to page 61)
and others, for a work with several authors, usually three or more
O'Keeffe et al. (2010) discuss this problem.

lesson.text: e.g. introduces examples; i.e. restates the same thing in other words. Mixing them up is one of the commonest mistakes in academic writing.

exercises.prompt: This helmet dates from 500 ___ . It's over 1,500 years old.
exercises.hint: (two possible abbreviations for years since the birth of Christ)
exercises.explanation: AD (Anno Domini) counts years since the birth of Christ; many people prefer CE, the Common Era.

exercises.prompt: The file extension, ___ the letters that follow its name, such as .docx or .jpg, tells you what type of file it is.
exercises.explanation: i.e. (id est) means that is - it restates something in other words.

exercises.prompt: Type your message here. ___ , press 'save' before pressing 'send', or you may lose your message.
exercises.explanation: NB (nota bene) is used as a warning or to point out something important.

exercises.prompt: Fruits, ___ lemons, pears or grapes, are sometimes added when cooking poultry.
Match each abbreviation with what it stands for.
Match each shortened or blended word with its meaning.

pairs.right: a humorous TV programme built on one situation
a film about the life of a real person
a flat whose one room is both bedroom and sitting room
a wireless connection for computers and phones
details of someone's life, job and achievements

exercises.prompt: If someone asks you for ID, what do they want?
options: proof of identity, such as a passport or driving licence

exercises.prompt: If a party invitation says RSVP, what should you do?
exercises.explanation: RSVP comes from French and means please reply.

exercises.prompt: If you see PTO at the bottom of a document, what should you do next?
exercises.explanation: PTO stands for please turn over.

exercises.prompt: If you are watching a sitcom, what are you more likely to want to do?
exercises.explanation: A sitcom is a situational comedy - a humorous TV programme.

exercises.prompt: Which is likely to be cheaper to rent in the same city street, a two-bedroom flat or a ___ ?
exercises.explanation: A bedsit has only one room, serving as both bedroom and sitting room, so it costs less.

exercises.prompt: If someone asks you to take an ___ test, they want to find out your level of intelligence.
He manages to get into the ___ lounge at most airports. I don't know how he does it.
exercises.explanation: VIP stands for very important person.

exercises.statement: Smedley and Jones (eds.) means that Smedley and Jones wrote the book referred to.
exercises.explanation: It means they edited it - they oversaw the contents and structure but did not write it.

exercises.statement: See pp. 33-37 means see the information on page 33 and on page 37 only.
exercises.explanation: It means all the information from page 33 to page 37 inclusive.

exercises.statement: Markov et al. means that Markov wrote the work with two or more other people.
exercises.explanation: Correct - et al. normally refers to three or more co-authors; if there are just two, both names are given.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Cf. Oswald (1987)' ask the reader to do?
options: note that Oswald edited the work

exercises.prompt: Is each abbreviation said letter by letter, or as a whole word?
